Priesthood of All Believers
PREES-thood of AWL bih-LEEV-urz
n. phrase (Reformation ecclesiology; doctrine of access)
From Old English preost (priest, from Late Latin presbyter, from Greek presbyteros, elder) + Old English aelra (all) + belīefan (to believe); Luther's summary phrase (1520, To the Christian Nobility) for the New Testament teaching that every believer has direct access to God through Christ, the one Mediator, without the need of a human priestly caste.

Biblical Definition

The priesthood of all believers is the New Testament doctrine that every regenerate believer has direct, unmediated access to God through Jesus Christ, the one and only High Priest, and exercises a priestly function in intercession, worship, and witness. Peter addresses the new covenant community with language drawn from the Exodus charter: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession — that you may proclaim the excellencies of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light” (1 Pet 2:9). The entire church — not merely its ordained officers — is a “royal priesthood.” John receives the same vision: God has “made us a kingdom, priests to His God and Father” (Rev 1:6). The language echoes Exodus 19:6, where God promised to make Israel “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” — a promise fulfilled in the redeemed community of the new covenant. This is not an abolition of church order — elders and deacons remain as distinct offices — but it is a decisive abolition of the Levitical caste that mediated between God and the people. Christ alone is the Mediator (1 Tim 2:5); because He has offered the one perfect sacrifice (Heb 9:26) and entered once for all behind the veil, every believer may “come boldly to the throne of grace” (Heb 4:16) — no earthly priest, no purgatorial intercession required. The 1689 LBCF grounds every believer's access in Christ's finished work.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Reformation teaching — rooted in 1 Peter 2:9 and Revelation 1:6 — that every regenerate believer is a priest before God through Christ, with direct access to the Father and the vocation of intercession and witness, without the mediation of any human priestly caste.

PRIESTHOOD OF ALL BELIEVERS, n. phrase. The New Testament and Reformation doctrine that every believer in Christ is constituted a priest before God, with direct access through the one Mediator, Christ Jesus (1 Tim 2:5).

Luther deployed this doctrine in 1520 as a demolition of the Roman priestly caste: if all believers are priests, then no baptized Christian is mere laity having no access; the ordained clergy is a functional office for the well-ordering of the church, not a spiritual caste that alone can approach God on behalf of the people.

The doctrine carries three positive contents: (1) Access — every believer may come directly to God in prayer and receive forgiveness through Christ without human mediation; (2) Service — every believer is called to offer “spiritual sacrifices” of prayer, worship, and sacrificial life (1 Pet 2:5; Rom 12:1); (3) Witness — the “royal priesthood” proclaims “the excellencies of Him who called you” (1 Pet 2:9), making evangelism a priestly function of every member.

The doctrine does not abolish the pastoral office. Elders are appointed to preach, teach, and shepherd (1 Tim 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9); their authority is real. But their authority is not sacerdotal — they do not offer Christ afresh in the Supper, they do not alone have access to God.

The Roman Catholic Church, with its ordained sacerdotal priesthood offering the Mass as a real, repeated sacrifice, is the contrary doctrine the Reformation called the church away from.

Key Scripture

1 Peter 2:9 — "But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:"

Revelation 1:6 — "And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father; to him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen."

Exodus 19:6 — "And ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation. These are the words which thou shalt speak unto the children of Israel."

Revelation 5:10 — "And hast made us unto our God kings and priests: and we shall reign on the earth."

Modern Corruption

Roman Catholicism maintains a sacerdotal ordained priesthood offering a repeated sacrifice in the Mass — precisely the priestly caste Hebrews declares obsolete; contemporary evangelicalism sometimes invokes the doctrine to resist all pastoral authority whatsoever.

expand to see more

The Roman Catholic theology of orders teaches that the ordained priest is ontologically changed at ordination — given a sacerdotal character that enables him alone to offer the Eucharistic sacrifice, to absolve sins in confession, and to serve as the necessary mediator between the laity and God. This priestly caste is the contradiction of the priesthood of all believers. The Reformers' point was not merely organizational; it was exegetical: Hebrews 9–10 teaches that Christ offered one sacrifice, once, that need not and cannot be repeated. A priest who “offers Christ” in the Mass is either repeating what cannot be repeated or pretending to an office that has been abolished.

Contemporary evangelical corruption runs in the opposite direction: the priesthood of all believers is sometimes invoked to resist any church authority whatsoever — “I don't need a pastor, I have the Spirit.” This misreads the doctrine. The priesthood of all believers grants every believer direct access in prayer and Scripture; it does not grant every believer authority to preach to the assembly, govern the congregation, or determine sound doctrine in isolation from the gathered church and its appointed elders. The Reformation did not abolish the pastoral office; it abolished the Levitical caste that claimed to stand between the believer and God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hiereus (priest, one who approaches the holy and offers sacrifice) + presbyteros (elder); the New Testament fulfills the Exodus charter (Ex 19:6) in the whole body of Christ, while Christ Himself serves as the sole, final High Priest (Heb 4:14–16).

expand to see more

Greek hiereus — priest, the one who performs sacred functions and mediates between people and God; in the NT, used of Christ (Heb 2:17) and of the whole body of believers (1 Pet 2:9; Rev 1:6).

Hebrew kohen — priest; in Levitical Israel, the mediating officer between God and Israel; the Levitical priesthood foreshadowed and was fulfilled in Christ's high priesthood (Heb 7–10).

Latin sacerdos — priest who offers sacrifice (sacer, sacred + dare, to give); the root of the Roman Catholic “sacerdotal” theology the Reformation challenged.

Luther's Priestertum aller Gläubigen — the German phrase Luther coined in 1520; the Reformation's shorthand for the transfer of priestly access from a caste to all the baptized.

Greek laos — people, the whole people of God (1 Pet 2:9–10); all believers are the laos — the Reformation restored their dignity by giving them direct access to Scripture, prayer, and God.

Usage

"The priesthood of all believers means that every believer who prays for another member of the body is exercising a priestly function — intercession is not reserved for clergy."

"It means that reading the Scriptures privately is itself a priestly act — the believer approaching the holy with no human mediator standing between."

"Rightly understood, it elevates the common Christian life: the mother who prays for her children, the layman who witnesses to his neighbor, the elder who intercedes for the congregation — all are performing the priestly vocation that 1 Pet 2:9 and Rev 1:6 announce."
